summary: An informational summary of the RFCs numbered 2500 through 2599, intended as a reference for people tracking what the series published in that range.

eli5.summary: This is a table of contents for one hundred documents in a very long shelf of technical books, so you can see at a glance what was added.

subtitle: A reference guide to 100 technical standards and protocols published between 1999 and 2000

tldr.problem: Finding relevant RFCs across a large archive is difficult without a guide that groups and describes them by topic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2599 provides an annotated list of all 100 RFCs numbered 2500 through 2599, with brief descriptions of each document and notes on whether they are standards-track, experimental, or informational.
tldr.outcome: Network engineers and protocol developers can quickly survey what was standardized during 1999-2000 and locate specific RFCs relevant to their work.

today: RFC 2599 was published in March 2000 and serves as a historical snapshot of the RFC series at that point. It has been succeeded by later summary RFCs covering subsequent ranges. The documents it summarizes remain part of the Internet standards and continue to be referenced and implemented.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2599 is an informational summary of 100 RFCs published with numbers between 2500 and 2599. It serves as a reference document for tracking what protocols and procedures were standardized during this period (approximately 1999 to early 2000). Each entry briefly describes the document and notes its status: whether it is a standards-track document (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, or Internet Standard), an experimental protocol, or merely informational guidance.

This type of summary RFC is periodically published to help the Internet community navigate the rapidly growing RFC series. It acts as an index and checkpoint, making it easier for engineers to discover work relevant to their projects without reading abstracts from the full Internet Official Protocol Standards document.
sections.eli5: This document is a list of 100 rulebooks and guides that were published during one year, with a one-sentence description of each one.

sections.title: Scope and Coverage
sections.content:
The document covers exactly 100 RFCs: RFC 2500 through RFC 2599, published in chronological order in the RFC series. The RFCs span from February 1999 (RFC 2502) to March 2000 (RFC 2599), though the RFC numbers do not strictly correspond to publication date. Most entries include a brief description of what the document standardizes or recommends, and annotations such as [STANDARDS-TRACK] indicate the document's status within the IETF standards process.

The document does not assign new categories beyond those already in the RFC series; it simply organizes them by RFC number and provides quick reference information. Engineers should consult the full RFC text and the Internet Official Protocol Standards document for complete and up-to-date status information, as the status of documents can change after publication.
sections.eli5: This list covers 100 documents, numbered from 2500 to 2599, published over about a year. Some are important standards, others are just suggestions.

sections.title: Major Topics in the Range
sections.content:
The RFCs in this range cover diverse areas of Internet infrastructure and application protocols. A significant cluster addresses network management and SNMP, including SNMPv3 frameworks, security models, and management information bases (MIBs) for specific technologies like ATM and SONET. Another major theme is security and cryptography, including public key infrastructure (PKI), DNS security extensions, certificate management, and Internet X.509 standards.

Additional key areas include routing and multicast (IPv6 extensions, multicast support over firewalls, and inter-domain route aggregation), protocol extensions (HTTP WebDAV, IPP printing, LDAP enhancements, and TLS for mail protocols), and transmission and compression (IP header compression, PPPoE, IPv6 over IPv4). Infrastructure topics like DNS, DHCP, and MIME round out the range, along with several experimental protocols and guideline documents.
sections.eli5: The 100 documents cover network management (how to check if routers are working), security (keeping hackers out), routing (finding paths through networks), and new ways to send mail and Web traffic.

sections.title: Standards-Track and Experimental Documents
sections.content:
A large portion of the entries are marked [STANDARDS-TRACK], indicating they are part of the official IETF standards process. These include foundational technologies like SNMP version 3 (RFCs 2570-2575), the HTTP WebDAV extensions for distributed authoring (RFC 2518), and many security-related RFCs addressing PKI and cryptography. Experimental protocols, marked with Experimental Protocol, include session-key management (Photuris), extended IP multicast tunneling, and emerging technologies not yet ready for standardization.

Informational RFCs provide guidance, document existing practices, or discuss implementation considerations—for example, guidelines for NHRP client developers (RFC 2583) and multicast firewall strategies (RFC 2588). A few whimsical entries appear, including April 1st joke RFCs (marked with their publication date), which are humorous but may contain useful commentary on protocol design issues or satirize flaws in standards.
sections.eli5: Some of these 100 documents say 'everyone must follow this,' others say 'you can try this if you want,' and some just give advice. A couple are jokes published on April Fools' Day.

sections.title: Notable RFCs in This Range
sections.content:
Several entries have proven particularly influential. TCP Congestion Control (RFC 2581) defines the four intertwined algorithms that remain fundamental to TCP performance: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery. DNS Security Extensions (RFC 2535) updated the earlier DNSSEC work (RFC 2065) to incorporate feedback from early implementers. Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) (RFC 2543) introduced a new signaling protocol for creating multimedia sessions, which later became central to Voice over IP (VoIP).

Others address important infrastructure concerns: Benchmarking Methodology for Network Interconnect Devices (RFC 2544) provides standard methods for measuring router and switch performance. IPv6 Socket API Extensions (RFC 2553) enabled applications to use IPv6 addresses portably. IP Multicast and Firewalls (RFC 2588) defined how security gateways handle group traffic. BGP/MPLS VPNs (RFC 2547) described how service providers could offer virtual private networks over a single backbone.
sections.eli5: A few standouts: one explains how the Internet slows down and speeds back up (TCP), another started VoIP, one says how to test routers, and others made IPv6 and VPNs practical.

references.text: Reynolds, J., Ed., "Internet Official Protocol Standards", STD 1, RFC 3000, November 2001.
